passage: Last spring I nearly bought a used scooter from Wasim, a mechanic two streets from my PG. "Eighty-five thousand, madam, almost new," he said, patting the seat. My first thought was that seventy-five would be a steal. Then I caught myself. Why seventy-five? Only because he'd said eighty-five. So I asked myself a different question: if I had walked in and seen this scooter with no price on it, what would I think it was worth? I honestly didn't know. That evening I checked two resale listings for the same model and year, and asked my cousin, who sells bikes in Nagpur. All three said around sixty. I offered sixty-two. Wasim grumbled, then agreed. I'm Devika, and I still ride it.

qa.q: How much did Wasim first ask for the scooter?
qa.a: Wasim asked for eighty-five thousand.

qa.q: Why did Devika stop herself after thinking seventy-five would be a steal?
qa.a: She noticed that seventy-five only felt fair because Wasim had said eighty-five, and she didn't want his number deciding the price for her.

qa.q: Which of Devika's steps could someone copy when a seller names a price?
qa.a: Ask what the item would be worth with no price on it, then get two or three separate comparisons, like listings and someone in the trade, before making an offer.

qa.q: How might Wasim see Devika's offer of sixty-two?
qa.a: Wasim probably grumbled because the high opening didn't work this time, but an offer backed by the market was hard to argue with.

grounding: Shows a young woman setting aside a seller's first price by imagining the scooter unpriced and gathering three independent comparisons before offering.

passage:
Supervisor's note, purchase team, Friday. Written by Arnab.
Kalyani handled her first laptop order for the new interns this week. The supplier opened with one lakh ten thousand per unit and called it a "special rate". I expected her to bargain down from there, as most new staff do. Instead she said she would reply by Monday. In her working file I later saw a line: "What would I pay if I'd never heard 1.1?" Under it she had three separate quotes: a second supplier, the government purchase portal price, and our own order from last year. All sat near eighty-two thousand. She went back with eighty-three and her reasons. The deal closed at eighty-four. Next step: I have asked her to show the method at the team meeting.

qa.q: What rate did the supplier call a "special rate"?
qa.a: The supplier called one lakh ten thousand per unit a special rate.

qa.q: Why did Kalyani ask for time until Monday instead of bargaining at once?
qa.a: She seems to have wanted to step away from the supplier's figure so it wouldn't set her starting point, and to find out what the laptops were really worth first.

qa.q: What made Kalyani's three comparisons useful?
qa.a: They came from separate sources, another supplier, a public purchase price and last year's order, so none of them was pulled by the supplier's opening number.

qa.q: How does Arnab see Kalyani's approach?
qa.a: Arnab expected her to bargain down from the opening like most new staff, and is impressed enough to ask her to teach the method to the team.

grounding: Shows a young professional asking what she would pay without the supplier's first figure and collecting three independent comparisons before deciding.

passage:
Thursday night
Omkar's studio quoted ₹90,000 for Tai's engagement photos. My first reaction: okay, maybe we can get it to 75. Then I stopped. Would I have guessed 75 if nobody had said 90? No idea! So I did the boring thing. Called two other photographers that Tai's friends had used: 45 and 55 for the same hours. Also asked Tushar, who shoots weddings in Nashik, what's normal. He said 50 is fair and 90 is "big-hotel pricing". Told Aai. She laughed and said I'm the only daughter who does homework for a party. Booked the 55 one; her candid shots are lovely. Weird how 75 felt cheap this morning.
Charu

qa.q: What did the two other photographers charge for the same hours?
qa.a: They charged 45 and 55 for the same hours.

qa.q: Why did Charu stop after thinking of 75?
qa.a: She realised 75 only came to mind because Omkar's studio had said 90 first, and she wanted to know the fair price without that number in her head.

qa.q: What would you advise a friend who gets a high first quote, based on Charu's day?
qa.a: Pause before countering, ask what you would guess with no quote at all, and collect two or three separate prices or opinions, like Charu's calls and Tushar's view, before deciding. 👍

qa.q: How might Omkar's studio see losing the booking?
qa.a: The studio may be surprised, since a high opening usually leads to bargaining near it; this time the customer came back with outside prices and went elsewhere.

grounding: Shows a young woman noticing that her counter-offer was pulled by the first quote, then resetting by gathering independent prices before booking.

passage: Tejas, you're scared of Bruno next door? Let me tell you about your Vinita Nani at your age. In our town, the milkman's boy got bitten by a street dog, and the whole lane talked about it for a week: the blood, the injections, the crying. After that I decided every dog in the world wanted to bite me. I crossed the road for puppies. I screamed at our neighbour's old dog, who could barely stand. Once my father asked, "How many dogs have bitten anyone you know?" I said, "Lots!" He made me count. It was one. One boy, one dog. But that one story was so loud in my head, it felt like hundreds.

qa.q: What happened to the milkman's boy?
qa.a: The milkman's boy got bitten by a street dog.

qa.q: Why did young Vinita feel every dog wanted to bite her?
qa.a: The bite story was retold for a week with vivid details, so it filled her mind and felt like something that happened all the time, even though it was one case.

qa.q: What did Vinita's father do that helped, and how could Tejas try it?
qa.a: He asked her to count real bites among people she knew, which showed there was only one. Tejas could count the gentle dogs seen on the street against any that actually bit someone.

qa.q: How might the owner of the neighbour's old dog have felt when young Vinita screamed?
qa.a: The owner may have felt puzzled or hurt, since their old dog could barely stand and had done nothing to frighten anyone.

grounding: Shows a child who, after one vivid dog-bite story, decides all dogs are dangerous because the memorable case feels common.

passage: The school van broke down, so Disha and her brother Anand had to walk the last kilometre home in the drizzle. At the corner by the tea stall, three street dogs lay curled under a cart. Disha froze. Two days earlier, a classmate had told everyone about a cousin bitten on the leg who needed a big injection. "They'll bite us," she whispered. "All dogs bite." Anand pointed. "Those three have slept there all year. You pass them every day in the van." "That's different," she said, gripping his sleeve. The rain got heavier. She made them walk the long way round, past the temple, adding ten wet minutes, and glared at every dog she saw.

qa.q: Why did Disha and Anand have to walk the last kilometre?
qa.a: The school van broke down, so they had to walk the last kilometre home in the drizzle.

qa.q: Why does Disha feel sure that all dogs bite?
qa.a: The classmate's story of the bitten cousin and the big injection is fresh and scary, so it feels more real than the many days the same dogs slept quietly by the cart.

qa.q: What small step could help Disha the next time they pass those dogs?
qa.a: Anand could help her count how many times she has passed them without trouble, and they could walk by calmly together, giving the dogs plenty of space.

qa.q: What is it like for Anand when Disha insists on the long way?
qa.a: Anand has to walk ten extra minutes in heavy rain, and may feel both annoyed and protective, since his calm facts can't beat her scary story.

grounding: Shows a girl who heard one vivid bite story deciding all dogs bite, even the ones she passes safely every day.

passage: Ever since the residents' group shared a clip of a boy being chased by a dog in another city, ten-year-old Zainab had refused to go down to the play area of their Tolichowki apartment block. "Moti will bite me," she said, though Moti, the watchman's brown dog, usually just slept by the gate and let the toddlers pull his ears. Rehana, her mother, sat with her on the balcony. "How many children here has Moti bitten?" Zainab thought. "None... but he could." "And how many times have you watched that clip?" "Eleven," Zainab admitted. "Everyone keeps sending it." Down below, her friends shrieked with laughter on the swings.

qa.q: How many times had Zainab watched the clip?
qa.a: Zainab admitted she had watched the clip eleven times.

qa.q: Why does Moti seem dangerous to Zainab even though he has bitten no one?
qa.a: The clip has been sent again and again, so it fills her mind and makes a bite feel likely, even though Moti only sleeps and lets toddlers pull his ears.

qa.q: How could Rehana help Zainab get back to the play area?
qa.a: Rehana could go down with her, watch Moti together from a distance and notice how he actually behaves, while skipping new forwards of the clip for a while.

qa.q: How might Zainab's friends on the swings see her staying upstairs?
qa.a: They may miss her and not understand why, since to them Moti is just the sleepy dog by the gate.

grounding: Shows a girl who keeps seeing one scary dog clip deciding the gentle colony dog is dangerous.

passage: Omkar, I've decided. Hemant is officially skipping the school trip to Mahabaleshwar. Don't laugh. Have you seen how many bus accidents there are? Every night my feed shows me another one: a bus hanging off a ghat road, a truck on fire, people crying at the roadside. Yesterday I watched maybe twenty clips. Twenty, Omkar! Buses are basically death boxes now. My dad says he's done that road a hundred times and it's fine, but he doesn't see what I see. And the city isn't any better. There were three videos of bikes crashing at signals just this week. Honestly, I don't know how anyone goes anywhere. I'll stay home and look at the trip photos. Safer.

qa.q: How many clips did Hemant watch yesterday?
qa.a: Hemant watched maybe twenty clips.

qa.q: Why does bus travel feel so dangerous to Hemant?
qa.a: Seeing crash after crash every night makes accidents feel common, so the number of clips feels like the number of real crashes. Dad's hundred safe trips feel less real than the videos.

qa.q: What could help Hemant check the real risk before skipping the trip?
qa.a: Hemant could ask how many school trips on that road had problems, find out how many buses travel it safely every day, and take a break from the clips for a week.

qa.q: How might Omkar feel hearing this?
qa.a: Omkar may worry about Hemant and feel disappointed about the trip, and might notice that the clips, not the road, have changed the plan.

grounding: Shows a teenager whose nightly feed of accident clips makes buses and the city seem far riskier than they are.

passage: I'm Afreen, Zubin's older sister, and lately I've watched my brother change. He's fifteen, and he used to cycle everywhere. Now he won't cross the main road near our flat in Pune without Ammi. Every night I hear the same sounds from his room: screeching brakes, horns, a crash, then the next reel. At dinner he told Abbu the city was "the most dangerous place on earth" and listed four accidents he'd seen that week: one in Jaipur, two abroad, one he couldn't place. Abbu said he'd driven here for thirty years without a scratch. Zubin just shook his head. I don't know if he's really scared or just caught up in those videos, but his cycle hasn't moved in a month.

qa.q: How many accidents did Zubin list at dinner?
qa.a: Zubin listed four accidents he'd seen that week.

qa.q: What does Zubin's head shake at Abbu's answer suggest?
qa.a: It suggests the reels feel more convincing to him than Abbu's thirty years of safe driving; seeing crashes every night has made danger feel everywhere.

qa.q: How could Afreen help Zubin get back on his cycle?
qa.a: Afreen could point out with him that the four crashes came from far-off places, suggest a short break from the reels, and ride a familiar route with him to rebuild confidence.

qa.q: What is it like for Afreen to hear those sounds from his room each night?
qa.a: Afreen seems worried and a bit helpless, watching her brother's world shrink without knowing how scared he truly is.

grounding: Shows a teenage boy whose nightly accident reels make his own city feel far more dangerous than it is.

passage:
Friday: Payal was excited. The whole class would take the overnight train to Goa for science camp, and her bag was half packed.
Monday: After a weekend of clips of derailed coaches and crying passengers, Payal told Vandana she wasn't going. "Trains are crashing every week," she said. "I've seen at least fifteen." Vandana, her best friend, asked where. Payal wasn't sure. "Everywhere. It keeps coming up."
Thursday: Vandana showed her a line in the newspaper about how many millions of people ride trains safely every single day. Payal read it twice. "Then why do I keep seeing crashes?" she asked, half to herself. She didn't unpack, but she didn't sign the form either.

qa.q: How many crash clips did Payal say she had seen?
qa.a: Payal said she had seen at least fifteen.

qa.q: Why does Payal ask, "Then why do I keep seeing crashes?"
qa.a: The newspaper line clashes with her feeling that crashes happen every week, and she is starting to wonder whether the clips, not real life, created that feeling.

qa.q: What could Payal try before the form deadline?
qa.a: She could compare how many crash clips she saw with how many trips happen safely, ask teachers who went on the camp before, and pause the clips for a few days.

qa.q: How does Vandana experience Payal's change of plan?
qa.a: Vandana wants to go on the trip together, so the friend tries patiently with questions and facts rather than mocking the fear.

grounding: Shows a teenager who, after a weekend of crash clips, believes train travel is far riskier than it is, over several days.

passage: Seema had won a summer internship in Delhi, and her uncle had already booked the flight from Kochi. But all week the TV in the Irinjalakuda tea shop had replayed coverage of a plane crash abroad: the smoking field, the weeping families. "I'll take the train," she told her cousin Jomon. "Forty-eight hours is fine. Planes are too risky." That evening she rode her scooty to the market to buy snacks for the journey, hair flying, her helmet hanging from the mirror. Jomon, riding behind on his cycle, shouted, "Helmet!" "It's only two kilometres," she called back, weaving past a bus.

qa.q: Where was Seema's helmet while she rode to the market?
qa.a: Her helmet was hanging from the mirror.

qa.q: Why does flying feel riskier to Seema than riding without a helmet?
qa.a: The crash coverage, with its smoke and weeping families, replayed all week, so it feels close and likely, while her short daily rides feel ordinary and safe.

qa.q: What would you advise Seema?
qa.a: She could compare how often people are hurt on scooters with how often planes crash, and start by wearing the helmet on every ride, however short.

qa.q: How might Jomon feel, riding behind her?
qa.a: Jomon may feel frustrated and anxious, since he sees the real risk right in front of him while she worries about a far-off one.

grounding: Shows a student afraid to fly after dramatic crash coverage while riding a scooter without a helmet.

passage: In their Madrid student flat, Valentina had spent three nights reading about a rare brain infection after watching a documentary about one unlucky swimmer. She stopped going to the pool and asked Mei, her flatmate, whether the tap water was safe. "The article says it's one in millions," Mei said. "But it happened to someone," Valentina answered. The next morning she was late for her exam, so she grabbed her bike without the helmet, earbuds in, and ran two red lights down the avenue, texting her professor at the second one. Mei watched from the balcony, coffee in hand, not sure whether to laugh or shout.

qa.q: What did Valentina do at the second red light?
qa.a: She was texting her professor at the second red light.

qa.q: Why does the rare infection feel so threatening to Valentina?
qa.a: The documentary gave her one vivid, unlucky story, and three nights of reading kept it in front of her, so it feels likely even though it is one in millions.

qa.q: What could Valentina do to put her caution where the real risk is?
qa.a: She could compare the odds of the rare infection with the odds of a bike accident, go back to the pool, and make the helmet and no-phone rule a habit on her bike.

qa.q: What is it like for Mei to watch from the balcony?
qa.a: Mei is torn between laughing and shouting, because the flatmate who fears a one-in-millions illness takes big everyday risks without noticing. 😬

grounding: Shows a student who fears a rare illness after dramatic coverage while cycling helmetless through red lights.

passage: In the college health centre's waiting room, Manoj kept scrolling news of a rare fever that had killed two people in another state. His forehead felt warm, he told Siddharth; his neck felt stiff. "It's all over the news." Siddharth had come on the back of Manoj's bike, and both their helmets were still at the hostel. "You rode at eighty on the highway with no helmet to get here," Siddharth said. "Roads are fine, I know the roads," Manoj said, still scrolling. When the nurse called his name, the doctor listened, examined him and said it looked like an ordinary cold. Manoj asked three more times whether she was sure.

qa.q: What did the doctor say Manoj's symptoms looked like?
qa.a: The doctor said it looked like an ordinary cold.

qa.q: Why did Manoj ask the doctor three more times whether she was sure?
qa.a: The rare fever news is so vivid in his mind that a simple answer doesn't feel believable; the dramatic story feels more likely than an ordinary cold.

qa.q: What could Manoj do to match his worry to real risks?
qa.a: He could limit how much fever news he reads, trust the doctor's check, and put his caution where danger is common, by wearing a helmet on every ride.

qa.q: How does Siddharth see the ride and the worry?
qa.a: Siddharth sees the irony: the helmetless highway ride was the real danger that day, yet Manoj only worries about the far-off fever.

grounding: Shows a student frightened of a rare fever from news coverage while riding fast on a highway without a helmet.

passage:
Family diary, Sunday. Irfan, Noor's abba.
Today the family group lit up again. Rehana's aunt forwarded a message about child kidnappers in vans "in every city". By lunch, three relatives had called Rehana, telling us never to take baby Noor outside. Ammi wanted to hire a guard. Meanwhile I noticed: the stair gate has been broken for a week, the cleaning liquids sit under the kitchen sink with no lock, and Noor's crib is right next to the window cord. Nobody mentioned those. What I did: I checked the city police's page; the forwarded message had been marked false last year. I asked the family, gently, whether anyone had real figures. Then I fixed the gate and moved the crib.

qa.q: What had been broken for a week?
qa.a: The stair gate had been broken for a week.

qa.q: What was Irfan worried about while the family panicked?
qa.a: Irfan worried that the vivid rumour was pulling everyone's attention away from real risks at home, like the broken gate, the unlocked cleaning liquids and the window cord near the crib.

qa.q: Which of Irfan's steps would help other families facing a scary forward?
qa.a: Checking the forward against an official source, asking whether anyone has real figures, and then fixing the ordinary hazards at home.

qa.q: How might Rehana feel after three worried calls from relatives?
qa.a: Rehana may feel scared and pressured by the calls, and then relieved when the message turns out to be false and the home becomes safer. 🙏

grounding: Shows a new father noticing relatives panic over a forwarded kidnapping rumour while ignoring everyday home dangers, and checking the real numbers.

passage:
Wednesday, 2 am feed done
Our daughter Mishti is three weeks old and my phone won't stop buzzing. My wife Parveen's mausi sent a voice note about a gang stealing newborns from hospitals, and now the whole family group is sure it's happening in our city. Ma wants us to keep the curtains shut all day. I felt my own chest tighten listening to it. But then, standing at the counter warming the bottle, I saw the kettle's cord hanging within reach of the baby bouncer, and the gas knob we keep forgetting to turn off. Nobody sends voice notes about those. Tomorrow I'll ask Ma, kindly, how many babies she actually knows were taken. And I'll tape the cord up.
Ujjwal

qa.q: What did Parveen's mausi send?
qa.a: She sent a voice note about a gang stealing newborns from hospitals.

qa.q: How can you tell Ujjwal felt the fear too?
qa.a: Ujjwal writes that his own chest tightened listening to it, which shows the rumour reached him even though he later questions it.

qa.q: What small steps does Ujjwal plan, and why are they wise?
qa.a: Ujjwal plans to ask Ma kindly how many babies she knows were actually taken and to tape up the kettle cord; this checks the scary story against reality and fixes a real hazard.

qa.q: How might Ma see the curtains-shut idea?
qa.a: Ma probably sees it as protecting her grandchild; the rumour feels urgent to her, so keeping the curtains shut feels like love, not panic.

grounding: Shows a new father seeing relatives panic over a forwarded rumour while everyday risks at home go unnoticed, and planning to ask about the real numbers.

passage:
Dear Kishore,
You asked why I cancelled my trip to Rishikesh after that rafting accident video and then un-cancelled it. Honestly, I watched it five times and my stomach dropped every time. I was ready to swear off rivers forever. Then I made myself stop and ask: how often does this actually happen? I found the state tourism report and a rafting association's safety data. Thousands of people raft there every season; serious accidents are rare, and most involve groups without licensed guides or life jackets. So I've rebooked, with a licensed company, and I'll wear the jacket they give me. It still feels a bit scary, but now it's a fear I've checked.
Your sister,
Sunaina

qa.q: What did Sunaina find to check the risk?
qa.a: Sunaina found the state tourism report and a rafting association's safety data.

qa.q: Why was Sunaina ready to swear off rivers forever?
qa.a: Watching the accident video five times made the danger feel vivid and close, so for a while one dramatic case felt like what usually happens.

qa.q: What in Sunaina's approach can others copy when a scary story shakes them?
qa.a: Pause, ask how often it truly happens, look at reliable figures, and then adjust the plan sensibly, like choosing a licensed company and wearing the life jacket.

qa.q: How might Kishore feel reading this letter?
qa.a: Kishore would probably feel reassured that Sunaina's decision rests on checked facts, not on one frightening clip.

grounding: Shows a young woman pausing after a vivid accident video, asking how often it happens and checking reliable figures before changing her plans.

passage: So, Jyoti, you asked for a story about fear. Last year a video went round of a lift in some tower dropping two floors. People screaming, doors jammed. I live on the fourteenth floor. For three weeks I, Ankita, the girl who hates exercise, climbed fourteen floors twice a day. My knees were furious. Then one night on the ninth landing I sat down and thought: how often does this actually happen? Next morning I asked our society office for the lift's inspection log, and read what the city's lift inspectors publish every year. Serious lift failures were extremely rare, and ours had been inspected last month. I took the lift that evening. Heart pounding, but I took it.

qa.q: What floor does Ankita live on?
qa.a: Ankita lives on the fourteenth floor.

qa.q: Why did Ankita climb fourteen floors twice a day for three weeks?
qa.a: The video of the falling lift was so vivid that it felt like it could happen any day, so the stairs seemed safer despite her aching knees.

qa.q: What did Ankita do on the ninth landing that others could copy?
qa.a: She stopped and asked how often it truly happens, then checked real information, the lift's inspection log and the city's yearly figures, before deciding.

qa.q: What might the podcast's listeners take from Ankita's story?
qa.a: Listeners carrying a fear from one viral clip might feel less alone, and see that checking the numbers can make a scary habit easier to change. 🙂

grounding: Shows a young woman noticing a vivid lift video has changed her habits, asking how often it happens and checking reliable records before going back to the lift.

passage: I'm Dilnaz, and I share a desk and a flat with Zeenat, so I saw this whole thing up close. Last month a colleague told a gripping story at lunch about an electric scooter bursting into flames in a parking lot. Zeenat went pale. That evening she listed her own e-scooter for sale. But then she did something I didn't expect. She deleted the listing, opened her laptop and spent an hour on the fire department's yearly figures and the maker's safety notes. She read some out to me: fires were rare, and most involved cheap chargers or overnight charging. Next day she bought the proper charger and moved charging to daytime. She still rides it to work. I'm not sure she's fully calm, but she seems steadier.

qa.q: What did Zeenat buy the next day?
qa.a: Zeenat bought the proper charger.

qa.q: Why did Zeenat list her e-scooter for sale that evening?
qa.a: The lunch story of flames in a parking lot was vivid and fresh, so for a few hours it made a fire feel likely enough to give up the scooter.

qa.q: Which of Zeenat's steps turned a scare into a sensible change?
qa.a: She paused before selling, checked the fire department's figures and the maker's notes, and then changed only the habits the figures pointed to: the charger and overnight charging.

qa.q: How does Dilnaz see the change in Zeenat?
qa.a: Dilnaz is surprised by the calm research and thinks Zeenat seems steadier, while honestly admitting not knowing whether the fear has fully gone.

grounding: Shows a young woman who, after a vivid story, checks how often scooter fires really happen and adjusts her habits based on reliable figures.

passage:
Dear Diary,
Two new boys came to our class today. Pranjal has round glasses and hardly speaks. He is definitely going to be the topper. You can just tell. Zubin is loud and made the whole back row laugh when Miss was writing on the board, so he must be weak in studies. I chose Pranjal as my partner for the maths quiz. Then Pranjal got three sums wrong, and Zubin got all of them right and even helped me with the last one. I think Zubin was lucky. Tomorrow I will see.
Afreen

qa.q: Who got all the quiz sums right?
qa.a: Zubin got all of them right and even helped with the last one.

qa.q: Why was Afreen so sure Pranjal would be the topper?
qa.a: Pranjal's round glasses and quietness matched Afreen's picture of a topper, so the look felt like proof even before any test.

qa.q: What could Afreen try tomorrow?
qa.a: Afreen could wait to judge until seeing how each boy actually works over a few days, and notice that the quiz already gave real evidence about Zubin.

qa.q: How might Zubin feel if he knew Afreen called him lucky?
qa.a: Zubin might feel unfairly judged, since he got every sum right and even helped, yet was still seen as weak because he is loud.

grounding: Shows a child assuming the quiet boy with glasses is the topper and the loud boy is weak, then explaining away the quiz result.

passage: At the village school near Sikar, Masterji asked the class to choose two children for the district quiz. Preeti didn't even think. "Mukesh," she said, pointing to the thin boy with thick glasses who sat quietly by the window. Everyone knew clever people looked like that. When someone suggested Vijay, she wrinkled her nose. Vijay was the one who shouted answers without raising his hand and played kabaddi every break. "He only makes noise," she whispered. Masterji held a practice round under the neem tree. Vijay answered eight questions; Mukesh answered two and blushed. Preeti frowned at the chalk tally, as if it had made a mistake.

qa.q: How many questions did Vijay answer in the practice round?
qa.a: Vijay answered eight questions.

qa.q: Why did Preeti frown at the chalk tally?
qa.a: She had been sure that Mukesh's glasses and quietness meant he was clever and that Vijay's noise meant he was weak, so the tally feels wrong to her rather than informative.

qa.q: How could Masterji help the class choose fairly?
qa.a: Masterji could pick the team from practice rounds like this one and point out that answers, not looks or loudness, show who knows the material.

qa.q: How might Mukesh feel being picked first and then answering only two?
qa.a: Mukesh may feel embarrassed and under pressure, since he was chosen for how he looks rather than for what he knows.

grounding: Shows a child assuming the quiet boy with glasses must be clever and the loud boy weak, until a practice round disagrees.
